q: What is Big O notation?
short: An upper bound on how an algorithm's running time (or memory) grows as input size grows, ignoring constants and lower-order terms.
detail: In ML: n samples, d features.
mistakes: Treating Big O as exact time.

q: Why is binary search O(log n)?
short: Each comparison halves the remaining range; the number of halvings from n to 1 is log₂ n.

q: List vs tuple?
short: List: mutable, dynamic size. Tuple: immutable, fixed, slightly more memory-efficient and hashable (if elements are), so usable as dict keys.

q: How does a Python dict achieve O(1) lookup?
short: It hashes the key to an index in an array of slots; average lookup, insert and delete are O(1); collisions are resolved by probing.

q: Why is NumPy faster than Python lists for maths?
short: Homogeneous typed data in contiguous memory, processed by compiled vectorised loops (and SIMD) instead of the interpreter handling boxed objects one at a time.
mistakes: Looping over NumPy arrays in Python.

q: When would you use a DataFrame instead of a NumPy array?
short: For labelled tabular data with mixed column types and operations like cleaning, filtering, grouping, joins and handling missing values; convert to NumPy for model training.

q: Name the inheritance types.
short: Single, multilevel, hierarchical, multiple and hybrid.

q: Compile-time vs run-time polymorphism?
short: Compile-time: overloading (same name, different signatures/operators), resolved before running. Run-time: overriding, where the subclass method is chosen when the call executes.
detail: Python mainly uses overriding and duck typing.

q: Map OOP concepts to agentic AI.
short: Class = agent definition; object = running agent with state; inheritance = specialised agents; polymorphism = execute() per role; encapsulation = private memory/goals; abstraction = simple methods hiding reasoning and tools; composition = multi-agent system.

q: Give an example of each complexity class in an ML pipeline.
short: O(1) cached prediction lookup; O(log n) threshold search on sorted scores; O(n) scoring all customers; O(n log n) ranking; O(n²) pairwise similarity; O(n!) brute-force feature ordering.

q: Your deduplication compares all pairs of 2M records. How do you speed it up?
short: Avoid O(n²): block/bucket records by a key (hash of normalised email, phonetic name) using dicts, compare only within buckets, or use approximate nearest-neighbour indexes for fuzzy matching.

q: Why is `if x in my_list` inside a loop slow and how do you fix it?
short: Membership on a list is O(n), making the loop O(n·m); convert to a set or dict first for O(1) average membership.
mistakes: Rebuilding the set inside the loop.

q: What is the time complexity of training k-NN vs predicting with it?
short: Training is O(1) to O(nd) (store data); naive prediction is O(nd) per query (distance to every point), improvable with KD-trees or ANN indexes.

q: Explain amortised O(1) append for Python lists.
short: Lists over-allocate capacity; most appends write into spare space, and occasional resizes copy everything. Averaged over many appends, cost per append is constant.
mistakes: Inserting at the front in loops.

q: Design classes for a multi-agent customer-support system.
short: Abstract base Agent (model, tools, memory, execute()); subclasses RouterAgent, BillingAgent, TechAgent; a Workflow class composes them; tools as injected objects; shared helpers as functions; interfaces typed for testing.
mistakes: Hard-coding the LLM client inside every class.

q: Inheritance vs composition?
short: Inheritance models is-a and reuses behaviour but couples subclass to parent; composition models has-a, assembling objects with clear interfaces, more flexible and easier to test.
mistakes: Inheriting just to reuse one method.

q: Why can NumPy single-element access be slower than a list's?
short: Indexing an ndarray creates a new NumPy scalar object wrapping the raw value; lists just return an existing object reference. NumPy wins on whole-array operations.

q: What is encapsulation and why does it matter for agents?
short: Bundling state with the methods that use it and hiding internals; agents expose execute() while their memory, prompts and tools stay internal, preventing accidental coupling.

q: Big O of common ML training algorithms?
short: Linear regression normal equation O(nd² + d³); gradient descent O(ndk) for k iterations; decision tree ~O(nd log n); k-means O(nkdI); naive kernel SVM between O(n²) and O(n³).

q: When can an O(n²) algorithm beat an O(n log n) one?
short: For small n, when constants or memory locality favour it (insertion sort for tiny arrays inside Timsort), or when the O(n log n) implementation is in slow interpreted code.
example: Timsort uses insertion sort for runs.

q: A pandas pipeline is slow on 50M rows. Options?
short: Vectorise (no apply/iterrows), use categorical dtypes, read only needed columns, use chunking, switch to Polars/DuckDB/Arrow or Spark/Dask, and profile memory.

q: How do hash collisions affect dict performance?
short: Many keys mapping to the same slots force probing, degrading operations toward O(n); Python randomises string hashes (hash randomisation) to prevent adversarial collision attacks.

q: What is method resolution order and why does it matter with multiple inheritance?
short: The order Python searches classes for a method (C3 linearisation, visible via __mro__); with multiple inheritance it decides which parent's method runs and makes super() calls cooperative.
mistakes: Calling parent methods directly instead of super().

q: How would you make agent classes testable?
short: Inject the LLM client and tools via the constructor (dependency injection), keep execute() pure given inputs, return structured results, and stub the client in tests, as with fake_llm in ex2.
mistakes: Calling the real API in unit tests.
